question: What are JSY and JSSK and could we use them for delivery?
answer:

JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana) is a safe motherhood scheme that gives cash assistance with delivery and post-delivery care, to encourage institutional delivery (INDIA-JSY, p. 3). In the Odisha guidelines, pregnant women delivering in government health centres are eligible. In accredited private institutions, only families with a genuine BPL card or SC/ST certificate are eligible (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). The Odisha cash amounts are Rs 2000 in total for rural areas (Rs 1400 to the mother) and Rs 1200 in total for urban areas (Rs 1000 to the mother) (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). An ASHA can help with registration, a JSY card and a birth plan (INDIA-JSY, p. 3-4).

JSSK (Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram) entitles every pregnant woman to free delivery, including caesarean, in public health institutions. This covers transport to and from home, diet, diagnostics, medicines, consumables and blood if required (INDIA-JSSK, p. 2). Free diet is provided for 3 days after vaginal delivery and 7 days after caesarean (INDIA-JSSK, p. 2).

Please confirm your state's rules with your local ASHA or ANM.

question: Is it okay to drink coffee while pregnant?

question: Can I fast for Navratri while pregnant?
answer: Thank you for asking before deciding. The passages don't mention fasting directly, so I don't have a trusted source on whether a full Navratri fast is safe for you. Please ask your doctor or ANM, especially at 26 weeks. What they do say: you need about 300 extra kcal a day, should eat more than your usual diet, and can eat 5-6 times a day if large meals are hard (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Your meals should include protein, iron and vitamin C, and fibre to avoid constipation (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). The guidelines also ask that family members support you in eating enough (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30). Your faith matters, and your doctor can help you find a way to honour it while keeping you and baby nourished. Please also don't take any medicine unless a qualified practitioner prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). If you ever feel faint or unwell, see a doctor promptly.

question: What are affordable iron-rich vegetarian foods for a pregnant woman in a small Indian town?
answer: At 17 weeks, simple everyday foods can help. Iron from plant foods includes green leafy vegetables, pulses and dry fruits (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Try methi or palak roti, vegetable idli or dosa (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34), and a daily dal. Paushtik khichari with rice, dal and spinach plus a little ghee or oil is a good one-pot meal (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Vegetarians can use legumes, beans and pulses in place of meat, fish and eggs (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Nuts and milk also feature in the sample diet chart (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 139). Iron from plants is absorbed less well, so add vitamin C fruits like guava, orange or lemon (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Avoid tea before, during or soon after meals, as it blocks iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Eating 5-6 small meals a day is fine if big meals are hard (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). You can also ask your Anganwadi centre about supplementary nutrition (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34). Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets.

question: My mother says drinking saffron milk makes the baby fair. Is that true?
answer: It's lovely that your mother wants the best for you and the baby. The passages I have don't say anything about saffron milk or about skin colour, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. What I can share is that the antenatal care guideline advises women to sleep eight hours at night and rest for another two hours during the day (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). It also advises refraining from alcohol, tobacco in any form and addictive drugs during pregnancy, and not taking any medication unless prescribed by a qualified health practitioner (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). It says that if there are taboos related to nutritionally important foods, the woman should be advised against them (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). Please keep up your regular check-ups, and tell your doctor if you have any worries, including about saffron milk.

question: What should I ask during my first ultrasound appointment?
answer: It's lovely that you're preparing. At 10 weeks, you can ask the sonographer or doctor about the things an early scan is meant to check (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. vii): 1) Is the pregnancy in the right place (inside the uterus)? 2) Can you see the baby's heartbeat (cardiac activity)? 3) What is the baby's size and my estimated gestational age? 4) Is it one baby or more than one? If more than one, ask about chorionicity and amnionicity. Also ask who will do the scan, since WHO says it should be someone with specialised training in obstetric ultrasound (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. vii). WHO recommends one scan before 24 weeks to estimate gestational age and improve detection of anomalies and multiple pregnancies (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). Details like the baby's head, spine, heart and placenta are more informative after 18 weeks, so you can ask when a later scan would be useful (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. vii). Some problems may not show on a scan, so it's fine to ask what the scan can and cannot tell you. For any specific concerns, please speak with your doctor.

question: Do I need Td vaccination during pregnancy in India?
answer: Yes, Td is recommended in pregnancy in India, and you're at 20 weeks, so there's still time. Under India's schedule, pregnant women get Td-1 as early as possible, then Td-2 four weeks later (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). If you already had two doses of Td/TT within the past 3 years, you need just one booster instead (INDIA-UIP, p. 4-5). Td-2 or the booster should preferably be given before 36 weeks (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). WHO also recommends tetanus vaccination for all pregnant women depending on past vaccination, to prevent newborn deaths from tetanus (WHO-ANC, p. 70). Pooled evidence showed a large reduction (about 94%) in newborn tetanus deaths with at least two doses, with no sign of harm to mothers or babies (WHO-ANC, p. 71). Some pain at the injection site can happen (WHO-ANC, p. 71). I can't see your vaccination records, so please tell your doctor or ANM about any earlier tetanus shots, and ask which dose you need now. Carry your vaccination card to your visit.

unsupported: Cutting out rice completely fixes gestational diabetes.
question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer: A high glucose result can feel worrying, but please don't panic. Treating gestational diabetes works well. WHO says management usually starts with lifestyle changes (nutritional counselling and exercise), and if needed, medicines or insulin prescribed by your doctor, which reduces risks to you and baby (WHO-ANC, p. 48). Sources say women with high blood sugar detected in pregnancy need referral and increased monitoring (WHO-ANC, p. 48), so please see your doctor soon to follow up on your result. I don't have a trusted source saying that cutting out rice completely fixes GDM, so I can't promise that. Our diet passages describe a mixed plate: cereals like rice combined with pulses and vegetables, as in paushtik khichari (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177), and eating 5-6 times a day. Please don't drop food groups on your own; ask your doctor or a dietitian to tailor portions of rice and other foods for you. Avoid any medicines unless prescribed (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31).

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer: Going to your parents' home for the birth is a lovely, common tradition, and wanting family around you is completely understandable. The passages I have don't say whether an overnight bus at 36 weeks is safe, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor before you book, as they know your own pregnancy. What the passages do say may help you plan: complications can develop at any time and aren't always predictable, so delivery at a health facility is recommended because it has staff, equipment and a referral system (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). Delay in reaching a facility is a major cause of maternal deaths, so arrange a vehicle and keep the ambulance number ready (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Labour signs to go to a facility for are a bloody, sticky discharge ('show') or painful contractions that grow longer, closer and stronger (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). So, whenever you travel, choose a facility near your parents' home, carry your Maternal and Child Protection Card, and ask your doctor about timing and the journey.

question: My family says the baby must be a boy based on my bump shape. Is that possible?
answer: I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. None of my passages say that bump shape can show a baby's sex, so I can't confirm it. What the sources do say is that fundal height (in cm) roughly matches the weeks of pregnancy after 24 weeks, and it shows how the pregnancy and baby's growth are progressing (MOHFW-ANC, p. 20). At 26 weeks, please keep going to your antenatal check-ups and let your doctor guide your care. Please also know that WHO notes that family preference for a boy exists in some places, and that some health workers choose not to disclose fetal sex after a scan (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 12). Whatever your family guesses, a healthy baby and a healthy you are what matter most.

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: Feeling anxious about labour at 31 weeks is very understandable, and you don't have to just be happy. Your feelings count. The sources show that you can have support and some say in how it goes. Health workers are expected to give emotional support as well as physical care during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can choose the position that feels comfortable to you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can eat and drink as you wish during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). A vaginal examination needs your consent, and the worker should explain what is being done (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Positions like standing, squatting or all fours can make pushing easier (MOHFW-ANC, p. 47). Women also say they value talking about their labour and birth with a health worker (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 17). So please share your worries with your doctor or midwife at your next visit and ask what to expect. If the anxiety is constant, stops you sleeping or eating, or feels overwhelming, please see your doctor soon. Perhaps your partner or a family member can come along and listen too.

question: My neighbour gave me herbal kadha for contractions. Should I take it?
answer: Thank you for checking before trying it, and it's kind of your neighbour to care. I can't say whether you should take this kadha. At 32 weeks, whether any herbal drink is right for you depends on your health and pregnancy, so please ask your doctor or pharmacist before having it. The national guideline advises pregnant women not to take any medication unless a qualified health practitioner prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). I don't have a trusted source on this particular kadha or its ingredients, so I can't judge it. Please show your doctor the exact ingredients. Please don't treat contractions at home; check with your doctor. Meanwhile, resting on your left side is advised in late pregnancy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31). You're doing the right thing by asking.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer:
Congratulations, and well done on getting through your C-section. My passages don't have C-section-specific home-help advice (like lifting or wound care), so please ask your doctor about that. What they do cover can guide your planning:

- The first two weeks are a key time to support your recovery and spot problems early (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xvi). Most serious complications happen in the first week, especially the first 48 hours (MOHFW-ANC, p. 59).
- Plan for check-ups: WHO suggests contacts at 48-72 hours, 7-14 days and week six. Home visits in week one by a skilled health worker or community health worker are recommended (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152; p. xiv). Ask your hospital or ASHA/ANM to arrange these.
- Decide in advance who looks after the home and any older children, and who goes with you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
- Ask family to keep the baby warm and help with feeding support (MOHFW-ANC, p. 59).
- Keep the 108/102 ambulance numbers handy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).

If you tell me who is at home with you, I can help shape a simple plan.

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: It's lovely that your mother-in-law wants to welcome your baby with something special, and it's kind of her to be involved. But the sources I have advise against giving honey or any other pre-lacteal feed before breastfeeding. Honey is named among the pre-lacteal feeds (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). Pre-lacteal feeds may not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections and diarrhoea, and it is a myth that something else should come before colostrum (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Your first milk, colostrum, is rich in antibodies and is all most babies need in the first few days (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding from birth to 6 months (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 148), and the Indian guidance says not even water (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). You could gently tell her that the doctors say your milk is the best first welcome, and invite her to share in cuddles, songs or blessings instead. If you're worried about latching or milk, please ask your doctor or a breastfeeding counsellor for support.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: What you're feeling is very common, and you're not failing. On day three, the thick yellowish colostrum comes in small amounts (30-90 ml), and the source says this is enough for a normal newborn's first days (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Almost all mothers can make more than enough milk if the baby suckles well, feeds often, and the mother feels confident (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Bottles, pacifiers, water or other fluids are listed as common reasons a baby may not get enough breastmilk (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 122). Feed often, at least 6-8 times by day and 2-3 times at night, in a relaxed setting (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). Let your baby finish one breast before offering the other (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). Signs of enough milk are good weight gain and passing urine about six times a day if your baby is exclusively breastfed (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Please ask your nurse, doctor or a breastfeeding counsellor to watch a feed and check attachment (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). See your doctor promptly if your baby seems very sleepy, is not feeding, or has few wet nappies. Gentle reminder: ghutti or gripe water is not advised (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80).

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Rice and rasam are comforting, but on their own they are not enough. The guidelines say a new mother should eat more food and fluids, and that families should not hold to food taboos that keep her from nutritious foods (MOHFW-ANC, p. 61). Food restrictions tend to be stronger after delivery and while breastfeeding, and she should be advised against them if they could harm her or the baby (MOHFW-ANC, p. 67). While breastfeeding, you need about 600 extra calories a day from a variety of foods. Eat 5-6 times a day, mixing cereals with pulses and vegetables, such as a khichari with green leafy vegetables and a little ghee or oil. Add daily green leafy vegetables, 1-2 fruits, and eggs, fish or meat if you eat them. Vegetarians can use legumes, beans and pulses instead (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). You can keep rice and rasam as part of your meals and add these foods alongside. Your family can help by making sure you eat enough and rest, without heavy work (MOHFW-ANC, p. 61). If you feel weak or dizzy, or your milk seems low, please see your doctor.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: Please don't worry about the Bengaluru heat. For the first six months, a baby does not need water. Breast milk has enough water to quench your baby's thirst, even in peak summer (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Extra water in hot weather is a myth, because breast milk contains all the water a baby needs (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). So at two months, feed on demand, at least 6-8 times by day and 2-3 times at night, and skip water or other liquids (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). If family elders suggest water, ghutti or gripe water, you can gently explain that ghutti and gripe water are not advised and may raise infection risk (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). If your baby seems unusually sleepy, feeds poorly, or has fewer wet nappies, or if feeding is difficult, please see your doctor. I don't have a trusted source in these passages on exactly how to judge that, so your doctor can guide you.
